transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Evelyn Carter (Quantum Retail - Head of ML), Marcus Diaz (CTO), Priya Singh (PM)

--- Auto-generated summary (brief) ---
Redwood walked through the Eval & Quality Monitoring console: how to upload prompt sets, define test suites, configure regression alerts, and run A/B comparisons. Customer asked about false positives, thresholding, how embeddings are used for semantic comparisons, and data residency/KMS. Agreed next steps: send pricing, security docs, and provision a trial workspace to upload prompt sets for a pilot.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: thanks everyone for joining, i'm maya from redwood, i'll run through the eval and quality monitoring demo today, jordan my se is on to do the deep dive on thresholds and the console
[00:22] Jordan: hey all, quick hi, i'll show the prompt set flows and how regression alerts are fired — and some caveats on false positives
[00:35] Evelyn: great, excited, we've been wanting a more automated way to catch regressions from model swaps and variant rollouts, right now it's pretty manual
[00:50] Marcus: our main things are: we need deterministic comparisons across model versions, quick A/B to validate behavior change, and low false-positive noise so SREs don't get paged late at night
[01:10] Maya: totally makes sense. i'll start with the high level — the console has a prompt set manager where you upload canonical prompts, tag them by intent/flow, and assign expected metrics (e.g., accuracy, rouge, business KPI proxies)
[01:34] Priya: when you say expected metrics can we plug in our own python evals? we run some custom scoring for rec sys relevance
[01:45] Jordan: yes you can. there are two paths: 1) run builtin metrics (bleu/rouge/bertscore/embedding-sim) or 2) upload a scoring hook — we sandbox it and run in our eval runners. note on sandboxing: long running jobs are rate limited
[02:12] Evelyn: okay good. what about A/B comparisons — do you route live traffic or do you replay historical queries?
[02:25] Maya: both. for initial testing we recommend replaying historical logs so you control the input distribution, then you can do a live traffic split for a canary A/B with traffic weights
[02:40] Jordan: demoing the prompt set upload now — notice we auto-detect duplicates, and you can mark prompts as canary/test/train sets; also you can group by feature flags
[03:10] [Minor audio glitch] Speaker 1: (unintelligible)
[03:22] Marcus: are regression alerts metric based only or can they be semantic (i.e., meaning drift)?
[03:36] Jordan: both. metric based alerts trigger on stat thresholds (e.g., 5% drop in em score) and semantic drift is detected via embedding-centroid distance and clustering changes — thresholding here is tunable, and we provide an initial suggestion based on historical variance
[04:05] Evelyn: how many false positives do you typically see? like, if we change tokenization or quantization we may get noise
[04:18] Jordan: good question. we've got a multi-stage filter: first, noise reduction via normalization and tokenization-insensitive embedding; second, grouping by semantic cluster so single prompt outliers don't create alerts; third, an optional manual approval gate before sending pager alerts
[04:45] Maya: and you can set alert severities — informational, warning, critical — with escalation policies to email/slack/pagerduty
[05:00] Priya: does the system keep previous model outputs for diffing? we want diffs for audit and some legal uses
[05:14] Jordan: yes. the eval runner stores model outputs (configurable retention) and you can view side-by-side diffs in the console, there's also export to csv and a replayable bundle for debugging
[05:35] Evelyn: data retention ties into security — we need to know how outputs are encrypted and where keys live
[05:45] Maya: about that — we'll send the SOC2 summary and the KMS/HSM integration notes. for private deployments we support bringing your own KMS and on-prem/private control plane options
[06:05] Marcus: that helps. on performance, when you run canonical prompt suites what kind of throughput do you recommend? we want to avoid huge costs
[06:18] Jordan: eval runs are optimized for batching; we suggest running daily regression suites at off-peak times, with smart batching to amortize token cost. the console gives cost estimates per-run based on tokens and instance types
[06:40] Priya: can we test quantized variants in the same flow for cost/latency vs quality tradeoffs?
[06:52] Jordan: yes, you can define model variants (fp16, int8, int4) and Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles based on your prompt length distribution and quality constraints. the A/B tool can route to variants and collect both latency and quality metrics
[07:20] Maya: showing the A/B comparison widget now — you can set traffic splits, define success metric (e.g., click-through rate or embed-sim threshold), and auto-generate a significance test for evaluation
[07:42] [00:07 background chat] Speaker 2: yeah that looks good
[07:50] Evelyn: on significance tests, do you support non-parametric tests for weird distributions?
[08:02] Jordan: we do. you can pick bootstrap, permutation tests, or standard t-tests; by default we bootstrap for metric distributions that are non-normal
[08:18] Marcus: what's the UI to drill into failing prompts? we want to see raw transcripts and classifier outputs
[08:30] Jordan: click the alert, it expands to show a failing prompt list with raw inputs, output diff, similarity score and a small replay button to reproduce the call in a sandboxed runner
[08:55] Priya: can we bulk tag prompts as "sensitive" so they get treated differently for retention and redaction?
[09:05] Maya: yes, tag-based retention rules are supported; sensitive prompts can be redacted at-rest and excluded from exports, and you can route them through private deployments only
[09:22] Evelyn: how do you handle semantic scoring for multi-turn conversations? some of our prompts are context heavy
[09:35] Jordan: we compute turn-level embeddings and a conversation-level centroid; the eval allows you to specify windowing (last n turns) and context length — also we maintain kv-cache alignment when reproducing to ensure outputs match production behavior
[09:58] Marcus: any gotchas with on-prem versus hosted eval runs?
[10:10] Jordan: hosted runs are easiest but data in transit goes through our control plane; for sensitive customers we offer private eval runners in your VPC or on-prem that run under your network and KMS keys — slightly more setup but same console UX
[10:35] Evelyn: ok good, what about integrations — do you push alerts to slack and integrate with jira?
[10:45] Maya: yes, alert sinks include slack, email, pagerduty, and you can auto-create tickets in jira with the failing prompt bundle attached
[11:00] Priya: walk me through the prompt set curation — we have 10k prompt variants and don't want to upload duplicates
[11:12] Jordan: the dedupe step uses fuzzy matching on normalized text plus an embedding similarity cutoff; you can tune sensitivity and mark families to sample representative prompts for the master suite
[11:30] [15 sec pause, keyboard typing noise]
[11:46] Marcus: one more security q — is there RBAC for eval artifacts and who can trigger replays?
[11:56] Maya: yes RBAC and audit logs — you can lock down replays to certain roles and every replay is logged with who ran it and which model variant was used
[12:10] Evelyn: great. in the event of a regression we want to automatically roll back. can Redwood integrate with our deployment pipeline?
[12:24] Jordan: we have webhooks and orchestration hooks. you can configure an automatic fallback policy: if critical metric drops by X% we pause traffic to new model and revert to previous variant — we can also trigger a ticket in jira
[12:45] Priya: what's the manual approval flow look like for alert escalation?
[12:55] Jordan: alerts can be configured to require manual approval before executing automated actions; approvals are handled inside console or via slack modal buttons
[13:12] [slight crosstalk] Speaker 3: um sorry
[13:20] Maya: quick demo of the regression timeline view — shows metric drift over time, correlated with deployments and config changes, highlights affected prompt groups
[13:42] Evelyn: will you run a small benchmark against our sample prompt set? we'd like to see how both base and quantized variants compare on our actual prompts
[13:56] Maya: yes we can. for the pilot we'll provision a workspace and you can upload prompt sets; we'll run a replay and do an A/B between your current model and the recommended variant. estimate is 24-48 hours for a full run depending on size
[14:16] Marcus: what's the expected cost estimate for a 10k prompt run? even a ballpark
[14:28] Jordan: depends on token length and model, but console will give you a cost estimate pre-run — rough ballpark for 10k short prompts maybe a few hundred to low thousands of dollars depending on model size and quantization
[14:45] Priya: can we limit eval runs to use only our reserved dedicated capacity? we don't want runs to hit shared hosted capacity and cause throttles
[14:58] Maya: yes you can pin runs to dedicated pools or on-prem runners; for a pilot we often recommend dedicated burst capacity to keep consistent runtimes
[15:12] Evelyn: any limitations on custom scoring hooks? compute time or external network calls?
[15:24] Jordan: scoring hooks run in a sandbox with CPU/memory and time limits; external network calls are blocked by default but we can allow VPC egress for approved hooks in private deployments
[15:40] Marcus: oh that is important. ok.
[15:45] Maya: final part — reporting and alerts history, exports and audit logs are all available; you can schedule daily digest emails for stakeholders
[16:00] Priya: great, i think this covers our main concerns. quick recap of next steps?
[16:10] Maya: i'll send pricing and provision a trial workspace, jordan will attach SOC2 + KMS notes, and evelyn will share canonical prompt sets and target metrics; then we'll run a benchmark and follow up with results and a recommendation for quantization/profile
[16:30] Marcus: please also include an architecture note for private eval runners so our infra team can review
[16:40] Maya: will do. thanks everyone for your time, we'll follow up with the pilot onboarding email
[16:48] Evelyn: thanks, bye
[16:50] [call ends]
